item.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3015
Authors: Miranda Christ, Oliver Korten, Tal Malkin, Noam Mazor, Shyamal Patel
Summary: Nearly five decades after their introduction, Merkle trees remain the most efficient hash-based vector commitments. They compress a vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ into a commitment whose size is independent of $n$, such that a verifier can open any bit $x_i$ using $\log n$ hash evaluations. The security of the scheme (intractability of finding two distinct openings for a given bit using the same commitment) follows from the collision resistance of the hash function. The verifier's runtime complexity is a bottleneck in many key applications of vector commitments, including SNARKs, credentials, and authenticated dictionaries. As such, a longstanding open question has been whether it is possible to construct hash-based vector commitments where the verifier makes a sublogarithmic number of hash evaluations.
We prove that sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible to achieve through black-box use of a hash function; we not only rule out constructions from collision resistant hash functions, but in fact show that commitment schemes with sublogarithmic verifier complexity are unachievable in the random oracle model. In particular, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers has verifier query complexity $\Omega_{\theta}(\log n)$, where $\theta$ is the input length of the random oracle. This bound is matched up to constant factors by high-arity Merkle trees. The key technical lemma in our proof is a disjoint product lemma, which can be viewed as a computational analog of the van den Berg-Kesten-Reimer (BKR) inequality. We believe this lemma is of independent interest, and in particular may be useful for showing other lower bounds and separations in the random oracle model.

item.title: Compositional, Computational Security Verification of the Signal Implementation Under Fine-Grained Compromise with Owl
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3014
Authors: Pratap Singh, Jacob Ginesin, Joshua Gancher, Bryan Parno
Summary: Key-ratchet protocols, exemplified by the Signal protocol suite, are at the core of widely deployed end-to-end encrypted messaging applications. These protocols rely on long-running chains of key derivation, in which fresh keys are continuously derived from prior state to encrypt messages. Their security goals include fine-grained secrecy properties, particularly forward secrecy (current messages remain secret under future compromises) and post-compromise security (the protocol can recover secrecy after a compromise), which can be difficult to reason about in formal protocol-verification tools.
We extend the Owl protocol-verification framework to provide computational guarantees of fine-grained secrecy properties for models that compile to practical implementations. Our extensions comprise a new type-based model of key derivation chains and a novel technique for reasoning about fine-grained secrecy properties via logical queries over the protocol's key hierarchy.
Leveraging these extensions, we apply Owl to Signal's entire two-party messaging protocol suite, developing high-fidelity models and proving its core security properties, including fine-grained secrecy. Owl's type-based methodology allows us to reason compositionally across Signal's sub-protocols, but still yields a full-strength end-to-end security guarantee. Owl's compilation pipeline translates our models into Rust libraries that interoperate with, and match the performance of, Signal's open-source implementations. We also extend Owl's methodology by directly verifying Signal's existing Rust implementation against Owl-generated specifications.

item.title: Fault- and Network-Agnostic Agreement
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3013
Authors: Erica Blum, Evan Hart, Vivek Malik, Aidan Mokalla
Summary: Classical fault-tolerant consensus protocols are typically designed for a specific timing assumption (e.g. synchrony, partial synchrony or asynchrony) and fault model (e.g., crash or Byzantine). We generalize the notion of a network-agnostic protocol to protocols that are agnostic with respect to network and fault type, establishing tight conditions on feasibility for a natural agreement problem across $\binom{2 \times 3}{2} = 15$ \emph{pairs} of classical models and comparing the costs and benefits of agnostic consensus with those of classical and mixed fault-tolerant protocols.

item.title: CHARTS: Compute-efficient Homomorphic Anonymous Routing with Tag Sums
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3012
Authors: Anthony Flath, Ke Wu
Summary: Anonymous routing is a fundamental tool to protect communication privacy by hiding who communicates with whom. Existing constructions based on a single untrusted router, including NIAR (EUROCRYPT'21) and the recent sPAR (CCS'26), typically rely on oblivious permutation or placement of encrypted messages, which incurs substantial computational overhead at the router.
In this paper, we present CHARTS, a compute-efficient anonymous routing protocol that eliminates the need for oblivious placement or permutation. Instead, CHARTS uses random tags and homomorphic aggregation to recover encrypted messages as an unordered multiset. Each sender encrypts its message under the intended receiver's public key and associates the resulting ciphertext with a fresh random tag. Using multiparty homomorphic encryption, the router computes power sums of the tags and tag-weighted ciphertext aggregates, from which it recovers a multiset of the encrypted messages. We prove simulation-based security against static semi-honest adversaries under decisional RLWE and an IND-CPA-secure, key-private, weakly robust public-key encryption scheme.
We implement CHARTS in Go using Lattigo. Our direct construction requires only homomorphic additions and evaluates a batch of 128 messages in approximately 260 ms of router computation, achieving a speedup of over 35,000 times compared with sPAR using its published parameters, on the same hardware and with the same thread count. We also introduce a factorized variant that reduces sender communication at the cost of additional router computation.

item.title: Non-Complete Set Coverings as Combinatorial Designs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3011
Authors: Oriol Farràs, Óscar Fidalgo, Carlos Andres Lara-Nino
Summary: Non-complete set coverings provide a combinatorial framework for constructing threshold implementations, a masking countermeasure against side-channel attacks. For a function of algebraic degree $t$, a family of subsets of the input shares yields a $d$-th order threshold implementation if every $t$ shares lie in a common subset and no $d$ subsets cover all the shares. In this work we study non-complete set coverings as combinatorial designs. We introduce incomplete coverings, a family of designs that contains non-complete set coverings and is closed under the dual complement operation. We show that coverage and incompleteness are dual properties under this operation, and we define reduced incomplete coverings, which do not contain redundant blocks nor redundant elements, two notions that are dual to each other. In addition, we prove analogues for incomplete coverings of classical properties of uniform coverings. Namely, we prove the existence of derived sub-coverings, a recursion rule for covering numbers and Schönheim's bound. We use these results to improve several lower bounds on the minimal number of blocks of non-complete set coverings. Moreover, we also find new coverings and upper bounds on the covering numbers based on enhanced algorithms, in particular for degree four and order three.

item.title: Practical Fixed-Plaintext Key Collisions on Reduced-Round AES
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3009
Authors: Stefan Kölbl
Summary: We study chosen-key collisions on reduced-round AES under the fixed zero plaintext $P = 0^{128}$, i.e., key pairs $K \neq K'$ with $AES_K^{(R)}(0^{128}) = AES_{K'}^{(R)}(0^{128})$. This setting directly affects the key-committing security of AES-based authenticated encryption and corresponds to one-block collisions on AES in Davies-Meyer mode with $IV = 0^{128}$. Fixing the plaintext locks the Round-1 input to $K^0$, coupling the cipher state to the key schedule in non-linear cycles that stall standard guess-and-determine rebound solvers.
On 4-round AES-128 and 7-round AES-256, we break these cycles using linear combinations of MixColumns rows and key-schedule columns that cancel coupled inactive S-boxes and isolate one- and two-byte non-linear equations solvable via small lookup tables. Combining this elimination with an 8-dimensional truncated differential space yields the first practical one-block collision on 4-round AES-128 with a fixed 0 plaintext in $\approx 2^{43.7}$ AES evaluations. On 7-round AES-256, eliminating all five internal conflicts together with truncated Round-7 matching reduces the classical cost from $2^{70}$ to $\approx 2^{38.3}$ AES evaluations. On 6-round AES-192, where the 6-word key schedule prevents sparse eliminations, we combine $\mathbb{F}_2$-linearization of active DDT entries with an interleaved meet-in-the-middle list-merging tree, achieving the first classical one-block collision below the $2^{64}$ birthday bound. We verify all three attacks experimentally and provide a colliding key pair for each variant.

item.title: Neon-HTLC: Collateral-Free HTLCs with Logarithmic Timeout
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3008
Authors: Sebastian Faust, Noemi Glaeser, Marius Hagemann, Ziyan Qu
Summary: Hashed time-lock contracts (HTLCs) are fundamental building blocks for decentralized finance, enabling trustless cross-chain asset exchanges and off-chain payment networks. However, standard HTLCs are vulnerable to bribery attacks, where malicious actors incentivize miners to censor honest transactions. While recent works propose incentive-compatible HTLCs to mitigate these attacks, they suffer from a severe scalability bottleneck: to secure a given payment amount, they require either a linear collateral or superlinear timelock (both in the payment amount).
We formalize this barrier by showing that the above tradeoff holds for a generalized class of HTLCs that we call "two-phase". Our analysis also identifies optimal parameter settings for two-phase HTLCs, improving on the previous state-of-the-art, He-HTLC (NDSS'23).
We then present Neon-HTLC, a novel incentive-compatible HTLC protocol that eliminates the need for collateral while drastically reducing protocol timeout. Neon-HTLC overcomes prior limitations by leveraging a novel punishment mechanism that increases exponentially over time. Consequently, Neon-HTLC achieves a timeout that scales only logarithmically with the payment amount. This timeout is not only asymptotically but also concretely practical: even for the total amount of Bitcoin, the required timeout is a small constant (max 51 blocks, or $\approx 8.5$ hours).
Our evaluation demonstrates that Neon-HTLC outperforms the state-of-the-art He-HTLC by several orders of magnitude: for a \$100,000 USD payment, Neon-HTLC safeguards the transfer in just 26 blocks with $zero$ collateral, whereas He-HTLC requires a 496-block timeout and \$5,000 USD collateral.

item.title: On the solving degree and complexity of Gröbner Basis computation over finite fields
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3007
Authors: Irene Di Muzio, Igor Semaev
Summary: Solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations over finite fields is a central problem in algebraic cryptanalysis, commonly approached using Gröbner basis algorithms. The complexity of Gröbner basis computation depends on the algorithm employed and is governed by the solving degree, defined as the maximum degree of the polynomials processed during the computation. Estimating this quantity is therefore crucial, and several bounds in terms of the degree of regularity have been established in the literature.
In this work, we investigate the effect of Buchberger's criteria on the elimination of redundant pairs, and prove that the solving degree of a Gröbner basis algorithm combining linear algebra with Buchberger's original algorithm is bounded above by the degree of regularity defined by the leading forms of the involved polynomials. This result provides a rigorous justification for using the degree of regularity in complexity estimates for Gröbner basis algorithms, thereby supporting a common assumption in algebraic cryptanalysis.
We refine the complexity analysis by establishing bounds on the number of pairs that must be processed. These bounds improve upon published complexity estimates, with particularly significant gains in certain parameter ranges.

item.title: Jacobi Signatures: Certified Chosen-Offset One-Wayness and Random-Offset Collision Resistance
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3006
Authors: Jinrui Sha, Bo Li, Hongrui Cui, Haolin Liu
Summary: Jacobi signatures are publicly computable vectors of quadratic characters whose security has primarily been studied for fixed consecutive offsets. We investigate two public-offset models under Balanced Repeated-Factor Factoring for honestly generated moduli $N = p^2q$.
First, we construct a total and compressing family on the full fixed-length Boolean domain and prove certified chosen-offset one-wayness. After observing $N$, the adversary may choose any publicly certified offset tuple, possibly with correlated coordinates, and retain state before a fresh uniform challenge is sampled. We establish a mean-fiber bound uniformly over all certified tuples and combine it with conditional-probability analysis and CRT/gcd factor extraction, obtaining a quadratic inversion-to-factoring reduction with polynomial loss.
Second, we construct a compressing family on canonical legal residues using independently sampled offsets. We state a shifted-Legendre separation bound in the legal-domain form needed by our reduction and combine it with the Jacobi/CRT collision-to-factoring mechanism to obtain collision resistance with negligible additive loss, without an additional Legendre-signature uniqueness conjecture. We further extend the construction to a total compressing family on a full fixed-length Boolean domain.

item.title: Time–Memory Tradeoffs for Message Modification in Step-Reduced SHA-512
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3005
Authors: Sitong Yuan, Hongbo Yu
Summary: SHA-512 is a core standard in the NIST SHA-2 hash family (FIPS PUB 180-4), and evaluating its step-reduced collision resistance is central to tracking its security margin. Recent collision attacks on 35–39-step SHA-2 rely on fixed-core two-block frameworks, where online message modification repeatedly connects random first-block chaining values to a fixed core and searches for compatible rear assignments. To eliminate the extensive chaining-value-independent recomputation on both sides of the core, we propose a coordinated front–rear time–memory tradeoff (TMTO) framework: on the front side, a shared counting directed acyclic graph (DAG) with online dynamic programming rapidly synthesizes batches of legal fronts; on the rear side, compact rear coordinates and bit-window bitmaps implicitly filter the step-16 compatibility relation without materializing huge tables. Under the uniform chaining-value model, our full front–rear TMTO lowers the expected online collision complexity of 36-step SHA-512 from $2^{66.2}$ to $2^{49.8}$ (7.05 GiB static storage), validated by a concrete standard-IV colliding message pair. At 37 steps, exact internal-branch unions further reduce the complexity from $2^{87}$ to $2^{75.2}$ on the public core (32.5 MiB) and $2^{75.0}$ on a new core (24.5 MiB). At 38 and 39 steps, although the rear space shrinks sharply, our front-side offline selection still applies directly to Gong et al.'s single-word-pinning attack, reducing complexity from $2^{100.7}$ to $2^{99.0}$ (38.1 KiB) and from $2^{131.3}$ to $2^{128.6}$ (3.11 MiB), respectively. All one-time preprocessing costs ($2^{23}$–$2^{29}$ compressions) are accounted for separately and are completely negligible relative to the online complexities.

item.title: SinCom: Shallow-and-Narrow Sinusoidal Composites for Low\\ Constant-Round Secure Evaluation of Activation Functions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3004
Authors: min yang
Summary: Non-linear activations remain the bottleneck in privacy-preserving machine learning: secure comparison is expensive, polynomial approximation needs many multiplication rounds, and the nested-sine construction of CRAfT is strictly serial---round count grows with depth, with no parallel ``width'' in which to buy accuracy.
We start from an asymmetry that holds across secure-computation back-ends---\emph{depth is expensive, width is free}---and ask for the shallowest, narrowest composite that still reaches high accuracy. The result is \textsf{SinCom}: a layered composite of MPC-friendly operators with depth $D\in\{2,3\}$ and per-layer width $W\in\{2,3,4,5\}$, joined by \emph{cross-channel weight matrices}, whose round complexity equals~$D$ independently of~$W$. Frequency is learned per layer rather than prescribed.
Unbounded activations must be split before they can be approximated. We single out a component that is bounded \emph{and smooth} and let the exact remainder be a branch-free skeleton, $f=x\cdot h(x)$; on softplus the split is instead the half-slope form $f=\tfrac{x}{2}+E(x)$ with $E$~even, and the optimizer places the skeleton coefficient at $c=\tfrac12$ on its own, beating the classical $c=1$ by up to $22.7\times$. Neither form is universal, so the outcome is a selection rule, not a single recipe.
At six sines the composite fits GELU to $1.4\times10^{-6}$, SiLU to $6.0\times10^{-6}$ and mish to $1.2\times10^{-5}$ (24-bit, $[-8,8]$); on CRAfT's own domain $[-3,3]$ with four sines it reaches $3.30\times10^{-7}$ on $\Phi$ against CRAfT's $1.62\times10^{-4}$, a $245\times$ improvement like for like. All figures are \emph{function-level}: the error of the composite in exact arithmetic, excluding what a distributed realization adds (\S\ref{sec:errmodel}). Parameters are public constants fitted offline, so a deployment ships the best of many fits at no online cost---which is why we report best-of-$N$.

item.title: EASE-SVM: An Efficient, Accurate, and Secure RBF Kernel SVM Framework for Medical IoT
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3003
Authors: Qingyu Mo, Wenyuan Wu, Jingwei Chen
Summary: The increasing use of machine learning in Internet of Things (IoT) environments facilitates more intensive data exchange, raising growing concerns about data privacy. Secure computation techniques address these concerns by enabling collaborative machine learning without revealing raw data. However, they often incur substantial overhead compared to plaintext computation, hindering their practical deployment.
We propose EASE-SVM, an efficient, accurate, and secure RBF kernel SVM framework based on multi-party computation techniques for medical IoT, covering both training and inference phase. For training, we exploit the fixed-value update property of PEGASOS to design an efficient two-party MPC-based kernel SVM training protocol that avoids generic secure multiplication. Under the evaluated settings, EASE-SVM achieves a $1.22\times$-$7.25\times$ speedup over the prior work of Mo et al. in the iterative training phase with a precomputed kernel matrix. For inference, we develop a privacy-preserving RFF-based framework that enables RBF kernel SVMs jointly trained by multiple parties to be distributed and shared without exposing their support vectors. To improve inference efficiency, we first develop an RFF parameter optimization method that allows both parties to optimize the RFF parameters locally using kernel values, reducing the feature dimension while maintaining approximation accuracy and classification performance. We also provide an optional decision-oriented variant that directly optimizes the approximation of the trained SVM decision function while incurring explicitly specified additional leakage. Additionally, we design a lightweight period-aligned two-party secure cosine protocol, achieving a $2.21\times$-$2.41\times$ speedup over the cosine protocol of Guo et al. (USENIX Security '26).

item.title: Where on Earth? Zero-Knowledge Proof of Location from a Phone Photograph of the Moon and Stars
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3002
Authors: Pavel Shuvalov
Summary: We study whether a single photograph taken with commodity hardware, such as an unmodified phone, can serve as a privacy-preserving proof of location. The physical anchor is lunar parallax. The Moon is close enough to the Earth that its position against the background stars shifts by up to about one degree depending on where the observer stands, so a frame that shows the Moon among a few stars, together with its capture time, determines the camera's position: one arcsecond of measurement error corresponds to about 1.9 km on the ground. Nothing is transmitted and nothing is received; the only infrastructure is the sky, a star catalogue and an ephemeris (a published table of where the Moon is at any given time).
We make three contributions. First, we measure what phone cameras actually achieve. Our study is based on 356 captures, of which 6 RAW frames give a position, with errors from tens to under two hundred kilometres. We analyse what limits the measurement and the ranges of capture parameters in which it is feasible. Second, we turn the measurement into a zero-knowledge proof. One proof binds a signed RAW file to a Merkle commitment of its pixels; a second proof recomputes the star centroids, the camera calibration, the Moon's centre and the parallax from the committed pixels, and shows that every position consistent with the photograph lies inside a public region, revealing neither the position, the photograph, nor the signing device. The prover is left with essentially no choices: the camera must be the least-squares fit to a complete, magnitude-limited star set, which cuts the prover's influence on the result from more than a thousand kilometres to under 25 km in our measurements. Six telephoto frames from one phone at two sites are accepted, with regions between roughly 370 x 370 and 710 x 640 km, as are three further test photographs, two of them published photographs from dedicated cameras. Both proofs run on two zkVMs; on the faster one the full pipeline for a photograph, ending in a zero-knowledge proof, takes about ten minutes of GPU and CPU time, and verification takes under half a second. Third, we analyse what the proof does not establish. A photograph of a laptop screen displaying a rendered sky is accepted as a proof for the original site, because the proof binds pixels to a signing device and its clock, not to the physical sky. We enumerate the trust assumptions, survey which device signals could narrow the gap, and outline measures that would raise the cost of more advanced forgeries well beyond the resources of an individual.
The result is a working approach for building location proofs from commodity-phone photographs, at country-to-region granularity, and not yet a complete proof-of-location system.

item.title: Representation-Aware Kleptographic Attacks on Post-Quantum Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3001
Authors: Sayan Das, Suraj Mandal, Thales B. Paiva, Prasanna Ravi, Debapriya Basu Roy, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Shivam Bhasin
Summary: Kleptographic subversions of cryptographic implementations, through Algorithm Substitution Attacks (ASAs), threaten the trust assumptions of black-box cryptosystems. This work studies such subversions in Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) through the lens of public-key representation. We formalize key-generation subversion with explicit public-key representations, distinguishing seed-compressed interfaces from expanded-key interfaces. This distinction captures a security-relevant role of seed compression beyond bandwidth and storage efficiency: public components regenerated from seeds can be checked against the specification, creating a regeneration barrier against certain expanded-component substitutions.
We further present the first kleptographic key-generation backdoor targeting HQC. Our construction instantiates the model in the expanded-key setting by building a BIKE-form in-band carrier that exploits structural similarities between HQC public-key formation and BIKE decoding instances. A subverter holding the BIKE decoding trapdoor can recover the randomness used to derive the victim's HQC secret state. We implement a dimension-aligned proof of concept and evaluate functional correctness, runtime overhead, and coarse black-box statistical tests. We further provide a conditional indistinguishability proof for subverted keys.
Moreover, we contrast this behaviour with ML-DSA, where recomputability from public seeds and secret-key material constrains analogous perturbation-style subversions. We also analyze a generic seed-level SETUP pattern as a remaining attack surface, showing that seed compression blocks certain expanded-component carriers but does not by itself eliminate seed-generation subversion. Overall, our results support the view that public-key representation should be treated as part of the kleptographic assurance boundary for PQC implementations.

item.title: LARK: Smaller and Faster Lattice-Based PRG
item.description:
Paper: 2026/3000
Authors: Yu Zhang, Jingnan He, Yijian Liu, Xianhui Lu, Dongshu Cai, Kunpeng Wang
Summary: A key challenge in designing practical lattice-based pseudorandom number generators (PRGs) is that such generators typically produce byte-oriented output, whereas lattice parameters do not necessarily align with byte boundaries, creating a tradeoff between fully utilizing each computed value and maintaining efficient byte-oriented generation. To avoid additional packing overhead, LEAP (FSE 2025), a state-of-the-art lattice-based PRG built on Ring Learning with Rounding (RLWR), retains only the lowest eight bits of each RLWR value for byte-oriented generation and discards the remaining high-order bits. Consequently, this high-order information contributes neither to LEAP's output nor its security. We present LARK, a lattice-based pseudorandom generator that directly exposes the low-order byte as pseudorandom output and uses the discarded high-order information as security-relevant hidden uncertainty. This additional uncertainty allows LARK to meet its target security levels with smaller parameters, yielding compact keys and efficient implementations.
To justify using the discarded high-order information as hidden uncertainty, LARK replaces LEAP’s RLWR-based output-generation component with one based on Ring Learning with Alternating Moduli (RLAM). For efficient polynomial arithmetic, we formulate RLAM as a ring analogue of the LAM problem introduced by Chen et al. (CRYPTO 2026), in which LWR rounding is replaced by direct reduction between coprime moduli. This modulus reduction introduces statistical bias, which LARK removes with lightweight masked rejection. We prove that LARK is pseudorandom under the decisional NTRU and RLAM assumptions. Compared with LEAP, LARK reduces key sizes by $42.85\%$ and $68.00\%$ at the $128$-bit and $256$-bit security levels, respectively, while consistently improving performance. LARK improves performance by up to $37.16\%$ in plain C, $10.55\%$ with AVX2, and $21.05\%$ with AVX512. In particular, the AVX512 implementations achieve $0.90$ and $0.91$ cycles per byte at the two security levels, attaining sub-1 cycle/byte performance at both levels.

item.title: Evaluating CNF/SMT Encodings for SAT-Based Differential Cryptanalysis of Lightweight Block Ciphers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2999
Authors: Marzieh Vahid Dastjerdi, Majid Rahimi, Iman Mirzaali Mazandarani, Sadegh Sadeghi
Summary: This study evaluates three encoding methods for automated differential cryptanalysis: (1) SMT formulations (using CVC), (2) standard CNF, and (3) size-optimized CNF (via Logic Friday). We assess these using four SAT/SMT solver types: single-core (CryptoMiniSat-v5, CaDiCaL), multi-core (Treengeling), and massively parallel Mallob—novel to cryptanalysis. Encoding-solver combinations are tested on seven lightweight block ciphers representing distinct design philosophies: SPECK-32 and CHAM-64 (ARX structure), SIMON-32 (AND-RX structure), PRESENT, GIFT-128, and MIDORI-64 (4-bit S-box in SPN structure), and LBLOCK (Feistel structure). For each cipher, SAT/SMT instances targeting specific rounds/differential weights were generated, with wall-clock solving time, parallel efficiency, and modeling effort measured. Our results establish criteria for optimal encoding-solver pairings that strike a balance between modeling simplicity and computational performance. Crucially, Mallob emerges as the state-of-the-art framework for large-scale automated differential cryptanalysis.

item.title: Differential Collision Resistance of Feed-Forward Sponge Variants
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2998
Authors: Ruixi Lv, Guozhen Liu, Shun Li, Siwei Sun
Summary: Feed-forward sponge variants have recently been proposed in independent lines of work to overcome the capacity bound limitation of the sponge construction and to strengthen provable (second-)preimage security. Representative examples include Sponge-DM, Sponge-DM$^{c}$, Sponge-EDM$^{c}$, and Sponge-F$^{P,pd}$. While these designs improve generic security guarantees, their behavior under dedicated cryptanalysis remains largely unexplored. Focusing on differential collision attacks, we review the inner and outer collision frameworks for sponge hashes and analyze how the feed-forward operation, the rate-capacity ratio, and the squeezing phase affect collision cryptanalysis. Our analysis shows that feed-forward sponge variants do not necessarily offer stronger collision resistance than the standard sponge, and that the modified collision conditions and the enlarged rate can even facilitate attacks. We substantiate this analysis on feed-forward sponge instantiations with Keccak-p that are configured to match the generic collision security levels of SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384, and SHA3-512. For these instantiations, we develop classical and quantum collision attacks. Compared with the best known attacks on the corresponding SHA-3 instances, our attacks reach more rounds or lower complexity in several cases. These results demonstrate that, for the reduced-round instantiations considered in this work, the structural changes introduced by feed-forward sponges do not carry over to collision resistance against dedicated classical and quantum attacks. They also indicate that strong collision resistance still relies on a careful choice of the feed-forward sponge configuration and on the differential propagation of the underlying permutation.

item.title: One Type Fits All: A General Analysis of Representation Trees for Subset Sum, LWE and Decoding
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2997
Authors: Andre Esser
Summary: The representation technique is the basis of the best known algorithms for random subset sum, of combinatorial attacks on small LWE keys and of information set decoding. It builds the solution in a search tree, the representation tree, whose analysis has so far required a combinatorial derivation by hand for every variant.
We introduce a general analysis technique for any representation tree, which replaces this derivation by a few short entropy formulas and turns the whole analysis into one explicit optimization problem, so that a new variant needs no new analysis. This technique alone improves the asymptotic exponents for almost all applications we consider. We then extend this analysis by adding filters, known from nearest-neighbor search, to every level of the best known trees and optimize them jointly with all other parameters.
Finally, we improve the filtering technique by partitioning the enumerated vectors into a sparse and a dense part, which lets the filters act in a more concentrated way, with significant gains especially for subset sum and LWE. Further, we reduce the number of optimization variables for the filters from quadratic to linear, which makes optimizations feasible that were previously out of reach.
Heuristically, random subset sum is solved in time $T=2^{0.2620n}$ and memory $M=2^{0.2120n}$ instead of $T=M=2^{0.2830n}$, and LWE keys following the distribution used in Dilithium are recovered in time $2^{0.2954n}$ instead of $2^{0.378n}$. We also obtain the fastest combinatorial algorithms for ternary LWE keys and LWE keys as in Kyber, the fastest algorithms for decoding over $\mathbb{F}_q$ for small $q\geq3$, ternary decoding with large weight, decoding with restricted errors and Lee metric decoding. Further, we improve on the best known algorithms for nearest-neighbor search over $\mathbb{F}_q$ and on the best known time-memory trade-offs for subset sum.

item.title: Real Brakedown Performance: A Portable Scalar Baseline for Spielman-Code Polynomial Commitments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2996
Authors: Jipeng Zhang
Summary: Brakedown-style polynomial commitment schemes encode the rows of a coefficient matrix with a linear-time Spielman code and Merkle-commit the columns. New schemes are typically compared against the unoptimized LCPC and PolyCommit libraries. Conversely, the reported speedups of the AVX-512 encoder SIMD-Spielman over LCPC combine vector arithmetic with portable algorithmic and memory optimizations. We present RBP-LCPC, an optimized implementation of LCPC in portable stable Rust that integrates column-major batched encoding, right-to-left graph evaluation, lazy modular reduction and cache-aware slicing. Its incremental structure isolates the contribution of each optimization. On both x86-64 and AArch64, its compiled hot kernels contain no vector arithmetic. With LCPC's code and prime, its encodings, Merkle roots and proofs match those of LCPC bit-for-bit. On an AMD Zen 5 server with one thread and N = 2^16 to 2^28 coefficients, RBP-LCPC encodes 8.14-9.06x faster than LCPC under its default build configuration. SIMD-Spielman, measured on the same server, remains 1.59-4.44x faster up to N = 2^26. Commit achieves a smaller speedup of 5.21-5.95x over the default LCPC configuration (4.48-5.95x across both default and tuned configurations), because column hashing then accounts for over a third of single-threaded commit time. Prove and verify are 1.83-7.61x and 2.65-5.36x faster than under the default LCPC configuration across thread counts and sizes, and single-threaded PCS setup is 1.31-1.44x faster. The accompanying artifact reproduces all baselines and measurements from fixed source revisions.

item.title: Improved GGM Witness-Encryption Bypassing Rank Gap
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2995
Authors: Charanjit S. Jutla
Summary: Hair and Sahai construct witness encryption in the classical prime-order generic-group model using a designed matrix space with a growing rank gap. We retain their encryption mechanism while replacing the minimum-rank requirement with a lower bound on the min-entropy of $Mr$ for nonzero matrices $M$ that do not permit witness extraction, where $r$ is the short random vector used in encryption. A matrix with substantial concentration has a column factorization from a finite family of short rational patterns. One list of linear forms evaluated at powers of a public random seed preserves all these patterns simultaneously, except with exponentially small probability, and therefore suffices in place of their multiple folded lists.
For a quadratic verifier encoding with $N$ Boolean variables, using $t=\lceil\log N\rceil$ forms gives one-bit ciphertexts of $\widetilde O(N^5)$ bits and optimized decryption using $\widetilde O(N^4)$ group queries. For sufficiently large $N$, distinguishing advantage on false instances is at most $N^{-\log N}$ against classical generic adversaries making at most $N^{\log N}$ group queries. Correctness error is $2^{-\Omega(N)}$, simultaneously for all valid witnesses of a ciphertext. At these same security and correctness guarantees, a beneficial reparameterization of Hair--Sahai's deterministic construction gives ciphertexts of $\widetilde O(N^6)$ bits and, with the same decryption optimizations, $\widetilde O(N^5)$ group queries.

item.title: Decoding Cost Lens: Cost Estimation for Code-Based Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2994
Authors: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Yuxuan Li, Qicheng Teng, Bo Pang
Summary: We present Decoding Cost Lens, a platform for evaluating the concrete decoding costs of code-based cryptographic schemes. It maps key- and message-recovery objectives to explicit attack instances, integrates classical Hamming- and rank-metric estimators, and provides quantum estimates for binary Hamming instances. The evaluation accounts for known block structure and applicable multiple-target effects under stated cost conventions. We apply the platform to 64 parameter sets from 15 first-round candidate schemes in the NGCC call for next-generation commercial cryptographic algorithms, comparing estimated work factors with the specifications' claims and security targets. Four schemes have classical decoding estimates below both the corresponding declared cost and the target for at least one parameter set. Zero-direction maximal minors (ZD-MM) replaces one guessed zero with a search over directions in a single block. For BAG-Loong, the lowest ZD-MM costs are $113.1$, $212.3$, $299.1$ and $386.7$ bits in increasing parameter order. ZD-MM also puts key recovery below target for BAG-Piglet-128 and -256 ($114.6$ and $254.0$ bits), and for all three BRA sets ($112.1$, $161.8$ and $316.8$ bits) after block transposition. For NSS-HQC, key and baseline message decoding costs fall below the $256$-, $384$-, and $512$-bit classical targets; the corresponding baseline message costs are $226.0$, $332.5$, and $440.9$ bits. NSS-HQC-128 also falls below its declared key-recovery cost while remaining above its target. The estimated quantum baseline message cost for NSS-HQC-512 is $251.6$ bits against a $256$-bit target.

item.title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2993
Authors: Raullen Chai, Xinxin Fan
Summary: Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to mt = 126 (TII-228, 2,463 CPU core-hours), with over 99% of runtime spent harvesting weight-(2t+1) codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves 1.0–1.5 GB of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. We pack 128 syndrome bits into one 16-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices (lossless for mt <= 145, and extended to mt <= 192 via truncated range pre-filtering), share G in {4, 8} cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch 64G random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix n' to cut modeled GPU-hours by 34%–47%.
Across five Track-2 challenges (mt = 108 to 153), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 (mt = 126) in 18.9 min (2.15 GPU-hours, 3.0x faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 (mt = 135, 22.1 L4 GPU-hours), TII-235 (mt = 144, 39.62 L40S GPU-hours, 17.97 s lift), and TII-185 (mt = 153, 140.4 L40S + ~60 L4 GPU-hours, 39.01 s lift). These results do not demonstrate practical recovery against Classic McEliece parameters (mt >= 768).

item.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2992
Authors: Zixuan Wang, ZHENG Tianyu, Yuan Lu, Bin Xiao
Summary: Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) let an authority be delegated through a chain of intermediaries and later exercised anonymously, as in DeFi credit delegation. Because presentation is the operation a holder repeats at every use, its cost is what matters in practice; yet existing DACs build this presentation from the delegation chain itself. We call this limitation prover awareness: to present, a holder must possess and process delegation-lineage material whose shape mirrors the chain. It has two faces: its size makes the presentation cost grow with the delegation depth, and its content exposes the holder to delegation-topology metadata that, in incentive-driven and compliance-aware settings, enables lineage-based policy vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship in otherwise permissionless networks.
We formalize the privacy face as Enhanced Delegation Anonymity (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness, the latter given both as a simulation definition and as an indistinguishability game over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Because both faces share one cause, the chain-structured credential, a single change of representation removes them together: our framework Proof-Carrying Credentials (PCC) replaces the explicit chain with a single recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC), making the presentation independent of the delegation depth and hiding the topology at once, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation. Unlike prior constant-size DACs tied to bilinear pairings, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits an explicit post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM from transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures.
On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 (non-post-quantum) instantiation keeps the verifier-facing proof constant at 7.344KB with 35-36ms verification across all tested depths, and a 128-bit Plonky2 (post-quantum) instantiation keeps a constant 157.9KB proof and 3.8ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03s per delegation step. Holder-side topology hiding and depth-independent presentation are thus achievable at practical recursive-proving cost.

item.title: A Practical Collision for 36-Step SHA-512
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2991
Authors: Junhong Huang
Summary: We give a colliding message pair for SHA-512 reduced to 36 steps, starting from the standard initial value. The first such pair was published by Yuan and Yu on 18 November 2026 (ePrint 2026/3005); we found ours independently four days later. The previous practical record had been 35 steps. The attack is not new. It uses the 36-step differential characteristic and the memory-efficient two-block framework of Li et al. (ePrint 2026/1120), whose estimated time complexity is $2^{66.2}$. Our contribution is to make it practical by: (i) counting the degrees of freedom and the uncontrolled conditions more precisely; (ii) re-solving $(A_0, E_4)$ on the fly for each first block, which makes the cost of the first block negligible; and (iii) a meet-in-the-middle lookup on 19 bits of $E_{16}$ whose table fits in the GPU's L2 cache. The collision was found after about 3 hours of wall-clock time on three NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (one RTX 5090 and two RTX PRO 6000), i.e. about 8.9 GPU-hours; Yuan and Yu report a similar expected cost and found their pair on 8,960 CPU cores in 16.9 hours. At the compression-function throughput we measured on the same hardware, this equals about $2^{49.2}$ evaluations of the 36-step compression function. The measured stage-by-stage pass rates agree with the cost model; for example, the step-22 survivors that also satisfy $\delta W_{23}$ number 9, against 9.3 expected. We verified the pair with an independent implementation, and independently re-measured the tail probabilities on $2\cdot 10^{10}$ generated message pairs.

item.title: Probabilistic Polynomial Time is a healer: Consensus with Mobile-Omission Faults
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2990
Authors: Julian Loss, Kartik Nayak, Kecheng Shi
Summary: We study synchronous Byzantine agreement (BA) with $t$ adaptive Byzantine corruptions and mobile, arbitrarily overlapping send and receive omission sets of per-round sizes $s$ and $r$. The adversary can selectively drop outgoing (respectively, incoming) messages for send omissions (respectively, receive omissions). Mobile means the adversary can choose a set of fresh send/receive omissions for each round. A well-known lower bound of Santoro and Widmayer (STACS 1989) establishes that time, by itself, is not a healer: any $c$-round agreement protocol with even a single mobile fault must incur an error of $1/[2(2n)^c]$. Yet, while this rules out deterministic protocols, to date, no \emph{randomized} protocol (even with higher probability of error) is known. This is all the more true when considering a model in which mobile omission faults are mixed with $t$ (permanent) Byzantine faults. Assuming $2t+s+r<n$, we provide the first protocols for and clean formal models for the mixed model with mobile omission faults. This matches the resilience of existing works in this area which consider non-mobile omission faults. We then build a player-replaceable BA protocol with subquadratic communication complexity, under the stronger assumption that $2t+s+r\leq (1-\varepsilon)n$.

item.title: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2989
Authors: Carlos Agulló-Domingo, Carlo Pascoe, Óscar Vera-López, Andreea Alexandru, Ahmad Al Badawi, José L. Abellán, Yuriy Polyakov
Summary: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively.
Our GPU implementation evaluates discrete-CKKS functional bootstrapping over a ciphertext with 64 encrypted Boolean values in 2.30 ms and with 16,384 encrypted Boolean values in 5.24 ms on RTX 4090, a consumer-grade GPU, whereas the CGGI programmable bootstrapping of one encrypted bit on the same GPU takes 2.16 ms. For 6-bit lookup tables, our discrete-CKKS functional bootstrapping takes 31.4 ms for 32,768 integers vs. 15.7 ms for one integer using CGGI. On RTX PRO 6000, our continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping is 3.5x to 7.4x faster than the best prior GPU implementation on the same GPU, while bootstrapping four to eight times as many values. Our continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping of the identity function, which corresponds to regular CKKS bootstrapping, takes 4.82 ms for 16,384 slots on RTX PRO 6000, the first reported bootstrapping latency below 5 ms for a CKKS ciphertext with this many slots. We were able to achieve such low latencies via a combination of algorithmic, architectural, and implementation optimizations, many of which were applied to both FIDESlib and OpenFHE. Our continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping also scales to larger ring dimensions, reaching 28.5 bits of precision with 23 levels remaining at a ring dimension of $2^{17}$.

item.title: A Note on Scalable Pseudorandom Unitaries
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2988
Authors: Giulio Malavolta
Summary: Pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) are efficiently computable keyed families of unitaries that are computationally indistinguishable from Haar-random unitaries; scalable PRUs allow the security parameter to be chosen independently of the number of qubits. Assuming quantum-secure pseudorandom functions and Vaikuntanathan and Zamir's conjecture on sequential Kac walks, we propose a construction of scalable PRUs. At a technical level, we show how to implement $n\cdot \operatorname{polylog}(n)$ steps of a sequential Kac's (pseudo)random walk by a quantum circuit of size $\operatorname{polylog}( n)$.

item.title: A Two-Party Threshold Signature Scheme for Aigis-sig
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2987
Authors: Li Wang, Tihong Qin
Summary: Aigis-sig uses Fiat--Shamir with aborts. Its rejection step depends on the full response, which complicates threshold signing. We present ThAigis-2P, a two-party threshold signature scheme whose outputs are accepted by the unmodified Aigis-sig verifier. The parties sample their secret shares independently from the Aigis-sig key distribution, subject to a spectral screening condition. Each party samples masks from a scaled hyperball and performs rejection sampling locally. The protocol runs K candidates per attempt. The spectral screening condition bounds the secret shift for every challenge and contributes approximately one bit of conditioning loss to the security reduction. The protocol has a three-round interactive mode and a preprocessing mode that exchanges commitments offline and requires one online round trip per attempt using committed salts and single-use records. In the random oracle model, the security analysis relates unforgeability to AMLWE under the Aigis-sig key distribution, MLWE under hyperball distributions, and the unforgeability of native Aigis-sig. The preprocessing mode also assumes a rollback-resistant state service. Experiments with a single-process C reference implementation based on PQMagic yield success probabilities of 0.22--0.25 per candidate and above 0.92 per attempt with K = 10. All 39,000 generated threshold signatures pass Aigis-sig verification. Canonical lossless encoding reduces partial response sizes by 21/%--25/% relative to transmitting raw coefficients. The evaluation covers all three Aigis-sig parameter sets and measures computation in a single-process prototype.

item.title: Threshold Hardened Derivation for BIP32-Style Wallets from the Hydra PRF
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2986
Authors: Cemre Özdoğan, Oğuz Yayla
Summary: BIP32 hardened key derivation computes HMAC-SHA512 on the parent private key and chain code. In a threshold wallet these are secret-shared, so the hash must be evaluated inside a multi-party computation. We present a hardened derivation that replaces HMAC-SHA512 by the arithmetization-oriented PRF Hydra. Once the PRF output is serialized, every remaining step is BIP32's; the derived keys still differ from BIP32's, so the scheme is a sibling of BIP32 and not wire-compatible with it. Both parent secrets form the PRF key, only public data enters its input, and every hardened child stays secret-shared and can derive further. We prove parent--child hiding, sibling independence, and hardened-child unlinkability by one path hybrid. Because the parent key is both part of the PRF key and BIP32's additive offset, the proofs need an offset-PRF assumption, which the published PRF claim of Hydra does not imply. The threshold protocol is proved UC-secure in the arithmetic-black-box model against static semi-honest adversaries, and with abort against static malicious ones, with no assumption on the PRF. With five parties under MP-SPDZ's malicious Shamir protocol, which our proofs do not cover, one derivation needs 243 rounds and 0.33s, against 15226 rounds and 3.3s for HMAC-SHA512; at 10ms round-trip time, this becomes 1.9s against 91s.

item.title: Coppersmith’s Method for Bivariate Modular Equations: Optimal Small-Root Bounds
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2985
Authors: Zhaopeng Ding, Yanshuo Zhang, Zhaopeng Dai, Ziyang Yan, Ying Chen
Summary: In 1996, Coppersmith established the classical small-root bound for univariate modular equations, which was subsequently proved to be asymptotically optimal within the standard Coppersmith framework. In contrast, a general theoretical characterization of optimal small-root bounds for bivariate modular equations, together with a method for computing them, has remained elusive. The main difficulty is that the additional degrees of freedom introduced by a second variable turn shift selection into a complex combinatorial optimization problem. We prove that, for standard triangular shift constructions in Coppersmith’s method, optimal small-root bounds for bivariate modular equations admit a unified characterization and can be computed effectively. To this end, we introduce a class of geometric objects called quasi-Newton polygons, which provide an exact geometric characterization of these optimal bounds and yield a method for computing them. This result extends the theory of optimal small-root bounds for Coppersmith’s method to the general bivariate setting, marking its first breakthrough beyond the univariate case in three decades.

item.title: Finding Optimal Small-Root Bounds for the Bivariate Coppersmith Method over the Integers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2984
Authors: Zhaopeng Ding, Yanshuo Zhang, Zhaopeng Dai, Ziyang Yan, Ying Chen
Summary: Since Coppersmith introduced his lattice-based method for finding small roots of bivariate polynomial equations over the integers in 1996, a general theoretical characterization of the optimal small-root bounds achievable by this method has remained elusive. In this paper, we resolve this long-standing open problem by providing rigorous proofs of optimality and an explicit method for computing these bounds. Specifically, using our newly introduced notion of quasi-Newton polygons, we rigorously determine the optimal small-root bounds achievable by Coron's lattice construction (EUROCRYPT 2004). We further prove that computing these bounds reduces to solving a univariate equation uniquely determined by the vertices of the Newton polygon. Applying our results to cryptanalysis, we systematically evaluate the small-root bounds reported in the literature for more than twenty cryptographic settings and prove that the vast majority of these bounds are optimal. We believe that our approach will help resolve further optimality questions in cryptanalysis and provide a theoretical basis for assessing the security of the relevant cryptographic schemes.

item.title: Four Dimensions Strike Back: Fast Isogeny Computation via Special Automorphisms
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2983
Authors: Jianming Lin, Chang-An Zhao, Yuhao Zheng
Summary: Four-dimensional isogeny representations enable fast signing in SQIsignHD (Eurocrypt 2024) and efficient key genera- tion and encryption in FastPOKÉ-4D, but their computational cost remains a bottleneck for verification and decryption. We present an algorithm that exploits two automorphisms of the structured abelian fourfolds underlying these representations. The first pre- serves the half-chain kernels and induces an action of the extra automorphism of Weil type (2, 2) on the intermediate varieties. With compatible symplectic markings, its action becomes a per- mutation of theta coordinates. This allows us to apply the two- point techniques of MIKE and propagate only two kernel repre- sentatives through the generic isogeny steps. The second automor- phism exchanges the two half-chain kernels. We determine the re- sulting middle involution explicitly as a Hadamard transform fol- lowed by a coordinate permutation, allowing the complete repre- sentation to be evaluated using one constructed half-chain and its stored dual-evaluation data. We apply this algorithm to SQIsignHD verification and FastPOKÉ-4D decryption. We also describe a fast heuristic SQIsignHD variant (denoted as F-SQIsignHDH ) with di- rect smooth-isogeny commitment generation, alongside an instan- tiation using Qlapoty for key generation and commitment. We pro- vide C implementations and compare the resulting protocols with their two-dimensional variants. Our experimental results demon- strate that, with the Broadwell implementation, F-SQIsignHDH gains overall speedups of 1.66×–1.92× compared with SQIsign-v3.0 in terms of the total running time of the signing phase and verifi- cation across NIST-I, -III, and -V.

item.title: Pethoa: Dynamic Proofs of Assets for Hidden Address Sets on Account-Based Blockchains
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2982
Authors: Yangrui Zhou, Dongliang Cai, Yuxuan Chen, Liang Zhang, Haibin Kan
Summary: Proofs of solvency allow custodians to demonstrate that their assets cover their liabilities, but conventional Proofs of Assets (PoA) often require publicly disclosing reserve addresses, exposing financial activities and enabling long-term transaction tracing. While zero-knowledge proofs can hide reserve addresses and prove asset ownership and balances against a public blockchain state, generating proofs for evolving blockchain states remains computationally expensive, particularly for chains with proof-unfriendly state structures. We introduce Dynamic Private Proof of Assets (DPoA), a framework for efficiently updating proofs of assets over hidden sets of on-chain addresses. Our construction separates asset-proof generation into an expensive initialization phase and lightweight incremental updates. During initialization, the prover establishes ownership and state membership for the reserve addresses. Subsequently, for each epoch, the prover locally updates its proof state based on newly finalized blocks and generates a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate the correctness of the update, avoiding the need to regenerate the entire asset proof from scratch. Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency of our approach: generating a conventional static proof for thousands of addresses takes several minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, whereas our dynamic update requires only a few seconds per block and runs entirely on a 14-core CPU.

item.title: Post-Quantum Self-Updatable Pseudonyms for Conditional Privacy-Preserving Authentication in VANETs From Lattice-Based Credentials
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2981
Authors: Rui Xiao, Xiaoying Jia
Summary: Authentication in vehicular networks must hide the sender and still allow an authority to identify it when needed. Schemes in which a vehicle derives its own pseudonyms avoid authority contact after registration, but known constructions rest on assumptions that quantum computers break. We present L-SUPA, a lattice-based scheme of this kind. The credential contains a binary key, and the pseudonym of an epoch is a vector of rounded inner products of that key with public pseudo-random vectors; because the rounding is an exact integer relation, the statement that a pseudonym is the rounding of the signed key fits, together with possession of a credential, inside the presentation proof of a practical lattice anonymous-credential system. Messages are signed with a fresh FN-DSA-512 key bound to the pseudonym, and a tracing authority separate from the issuer identifies a sender by scanning stored keys. The relation raises the presentation proof from $79.6$ to $81.4$ KiB and its verification time by about $3\%$; on one desktop core a presentation verifies in $0.15$ s, the time of about $4500$ message-signature verifications, and a message signature verifies in $0.033$ ms. A presentation adds $0.32\%$ to the message bytes of a one-hour epoch at $10$ Hz for $722$-byte messages, the most favorable rate, and messages of one vehicle are linkable within an epoch. The analysis states, goal by goal, whether we have a reduction, a conditional reduction, or a sketch; under the generic hybrid the presentation-layer M-LWE and LWR terms leave margins of about $80$ and $176$ bits for $2^{30}$ vehicles over ten years (no claim of $128$-bit anonymity).

item.title: Ties, Splits and Neighborhoods: New Area Records for Low-Latency Linear Layers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2980
Authors: Mostafa Taha, Arash Reyhani-Masoleh
Summary: For the 23 linear layers of the benchmark of Shi, Feng and Xu (SFX23, ToSC 2023), we search for minimum-depth circuits with the fewest 2-input XOR (XOR2) gates, and for minimum-area circuits at the same depth using both XOR2 and 3-input XOR (XOR3) gates, as in HILL by Li et al. (ToSC 2026). We combine three known techniques for the shortest linear program under a depth bound: (i) a beam search over the near-ties of the depth-bounded Boyar-Peralta heuristic; (ii) backward splitting; and (iii) a large neighborhood search. We set new records for the XOR2 count at the minimum depth for 14 of the 20 distinct problems represented by the 23 matrices up to row and column permutations, by 1 to 4 gates. After merging gates into XOR3 gates, our circuits are smaller than both the published XOR2/XOR3 circuits of HILL and the circuits of SFX23 merged in the same way for 19 of the 20 problems (UMC 180nm unit areas). We release the code, the logs, all the circuits recorded during our runs, and the verification scripts.

item.title: Chosen-Ciphertext Security for Nested Proxy Re-Encryption with Restricted Key Exposure
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2979
Authors: Haotian Yin, Jie Zhang
Summary: Proxy re-encryption (PRE) allows an authorised proxy to re-encrypt ciphertexts for another recipient without learning their plaintexts. We construct a single-hop PRE scheme with restricted chosen-ciphertext security (rCCA2). For a given honest delegator, an adversary that obtains an outgoing re-encryption key cannot also obtain re-encryptions to corrupted recipients. We revisit the nested encryption of Ivan and Dodis (NDSS 2003) with the encrypted delivery of the inner secret key described by Ateniese et al. (ACM TISSEC 2006). A recipient can recover this key from one authorised delivery and use it to decrypt inner ciphertexts sent to others. Encrypting each inner ciphertext under an independent public key of its intended recipient gives a scheme secure against restricted honest re-encryption attacks (rHRA). To obtain rCCA2, we use CCA2-secure public-key encryption, authenticate source ciphertexts and encrypted inner secret keys with strongly unforgeable signatures, and protect inner ciphertexts with deterministic authenticated encryption during re-encryption. We instantiate rCCA2 using hybrid public-key encryption with ML-KEM, ML-DSA signatures, and AES-SIV, and give key and ciphertext sizes. A packet-level OpenPGP prototype forwards the session key in a separate envelope and verifies decryption of the same encrypted body by the original and forwarding recipients.

item.title: SPAN: Privacy-Preserving Proofs of Sustained Aggregate Holdings in UTXO Privacy Pools
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2978
Authors: Zonglun Li, Xue Liu
Summary: Privacy pools are expanding from private transfers to tokenized real-world assets and holding-dependent rewards. These applications motivate evidence of sustained holdings across note replacements. We define a privacy-preserving interval proof of holding (PP-IPoH) scheme and present SPAN for arbitrary-value unspent transaction output (UTXO) pools. Two incrementally verifiable computations (IVCs) authenticate selected records and establish spend completeness, certifying a balance lower bound after every finalized transaction. An independent zero-knowledge succinct argument proves that this bound meets a threshold throughout an interval and supports subsequent queries over the same certified history. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness, and privacy under the stated component and ledger conditions. Experiments show linear proving time, adding about 2.9 seconds per additional transaction, and essentially constant maximum memory usage near 3.8 GB.

item.title: Which Masks Are Worth Testing? Key-Dependent Correlation and Symmetry in Lightweight Block Ciphers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2977
Authors: Alireza Gholizadeh Shahrbejari, Reza Ebrahimi Atani
Summary: The quality of a differential--linear candidate and the cost of selecting one are separate questions. We study both in reduced-round lightweight block ciphers. First, for 11-round CRAFT, we compare an alternative output mask with the published mask of Zhou et al. at the same input difference. In a paired study with 128 master keys, the alternative increases the observed mean signed correlation by factors of 1.69 to 1.86 across four tweak settings. Approximate simultaneous 95% confidence intervals for the four mean differences lie above zero. A separate held out study of ranking rules selects two distinct masks and gives inconclusive simultaneous intervals for detection-rate gains at a fixed data budget. Second, for restricted two-round linear sections, we use cell permutations to identify masks with the same distribution of absolute correlation over keys. We observe reductions in the number of evaluated masks in MIDORI-64 and QARMA-64. For three symmetric QARMA-64 cases, 81 masks reduce to 21, 45, and 36 representatives. Exact evaluation agrees with exhaustive search for RMS, stability, lower-tail, and threshold coverage objectives. The tested coordinate-permutation family gives only the identity in the selected SKINNY-64-64 section.

item.title: Authority Without Priority: The Revocation Trilemma and the Price of Stablecoin Freezes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2976
Authors: Di Wu, Yuman Bai, Shoupeng Ren, Xinyu Zhang, Yiyue Cao, Yuheng Wang, Xuechao Wang, Huan Huo, Wu Wen, Jian Liu
Summary: Stablecoin contracts let issuers freeze an address, but a freeze is an ordinary transaction that block producers order like any other, so a transfer submitted after it can still execute first. We define the missing guarantee as $\textit{revocation priority}$: once a restriction is submitted, no prohibited operation submitted later takes effect before it. We prove a trilemma: with revenue-maximizing block producers, no blockchain platform can provide revocation priority together with immediacy, which makes a transfer’s effects usable upon inclusion, and neutrality, which rules out preferential inclusion or ordering for any sender. Ethereum keeps immediacy and neutrality and gives up revocation priority. Using USDT and USDC freezes on Ethereum from 2017 to 2026, we examine how issuers and their targets compete for execution order. In one case, a freeze had long been pending when a transfer submitted after it executed first. The competition has escalated from fee bidding to private submission to execution delegated through intent-based orders. Overall, the issuer pays more for order than its target. These patterns follow from the two sides’ incentives, which we model as a Tullock contest. In equilibrium the issuer outbids its target but cannot buy certainty. Stricter freeze obligations thus strengthen its incentive to integrate into ordering infrastructure, at the expense of neutrality.

item.title: Exact Five-Class Paley Offsets and Sharper Nonlinearity Bounds Exceeding the Patterson-Wiedemann Direct-Sum Threshold
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2975
Authors: Filipe Martins Vono, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo, Valéria Gonzaga Santos
Summary: In a recent landmark preprint (IACR ePrint 2026/2680), Tang and Maitra established the first explicit fixed-dimension improvement over the Patterson-Wiedemann direct-sum nonlinearity bound N_PW(n) = 2^(n-1) - 27*2^((n-11)/2) = N_BC(n) + 81920*2^((n-39)/2), proving the existence of (balanced) Boolean functions in n = 375 variables--and hence every odd n >= 375--with nonlinearity exceeding N_BC(n) + 81921*2^((n-39)/2). Their framework combines index-two Gauss-period offsets on multiplicative cosets of GF(2^n)* with an unequal-threshold linear-feasibility criterion of Reis and Song and a sampling-without-replacement balancing lemma. Building directly on Tang and Maitra's framework, we make four contributions. First, we prove an elementary closed-form theorem showing that, for every prime q = 3 (mod 4) with n = ord_q(2) = (q-1)/2 odd and Gauss sum G_1 = 2^((n-h)/2-1)*(a + b*i*sqrt(q)) (b > 0, sigma = sgn(a)), the unmodified translated quadratic-residue template S = c + sigma*R (with Legendre symbol e_c = sigma) produces an exact universal five-class offset magnitude distribution, eliminating case-by-case enumeration. Second, evaluating the Reis-Song potential directly on the unmodified template S = 3 - R at n = 375 (q = 751) sharpens the certified threshold from C = 1.193239 to C = 1.192508, yielding NL(f) > 2^(n-1) - 442096*2^((n-39)/2) = N_BC(n) + 82192*2^((n-39)/2) for every odd n >= 375 (both unbalanced and balanced)--enlarging the strict margin above N_PW(n) from 2^((n-39)/2) to 272*2^((n-39)/2) while simplifying the construction to zero label exchanges. An exhaustive check over all 140,625 weight-preserving single exchanges confirms that 3 - R is locally optimal for the potential at n = 375; by contrast, at n = 431 (q = 863), where the isolated class carries 51.8% of the potential, two potential-guided exchanges strictly improve the threshold from C = 1.184952 to C = 1.183620. Third, a complete Hensel-Cornacchia screening of all 208 prime-order index-two candidates in 375 <= n <= 5000 produces an explicit monotone hierarchy of certified bounds--reaching NL(f) > 2^(n-1) - 26*2^((n-11)/2) at n >= 743 and NL(f) > 2^(n-1) - 24*2^((n-11)/2) at n >= 4935, closing 69.38% of the normalized gap between the Patterson-Wiedemann constant and Schmidt's asymptotic limit. Fourth, we establish a structural lower bound q >= 713 for single-coset Reis-Song feasibility and summarize a Stickelberger-LLL screening of higher-index primes below n = 375. All numerical inequalities are certified by exact integer and rational arithmetic.

item.title: Beyond Heavy Cryptography: Practical Private Vector Search
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2974
Authors: Chen Gong, Xiangyu Wang, Dan Zhu, Yuanbo Guo, Chunjie Cao, Jianfeng Ma
Summary: Driven by the explosion of AI applications, private vector search has recently gained widespread attention, but it still faces performance bottlenecks. Graph-based private search systems (Zhu et al., OSDI 2025) suffer from multi-round communication latency, while IVF-based systems (Henzinger et al., SOSP 2023) incur recall degradation and heavy computational overhead. In this paper, we propose EHSearch, a single-round, high-throughput private vector search system on encrypted data. EHSearch introduces HGI, an index structure that distills the HNSW graph into fixed-size groups, preserving local navigability for high recall. To avoid heavy cryptographic primitives, EHSearch presents Compute-Free Encrypted Filtering, which couples binary quantization with block-scoped pigeonhole matching, reducing the server workload from dense encrypted arithmetic to lightweight exact lookups. Extensive evaluations across four real-world datasets demonstrate that EHSearch outperforms state-of-the-art private baselines by 2 to 5 orders of magnitude in throughput, and scales out-of-core to 1 billion vectors on a single SSD. Specifically, when achieving 90\% Recall@10 on 1 million points, EHSearch answers a private vector search in 22.35ms P99 latency in LAN, and sustains 223.3ms P99 latency in WAN environments.

item.title: A Core-Spectral Theory of Differential Hull Clustering in Nibble SPNs: Improved Differential Distinguishers for CRAFT
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2973
Authors: Weipeng Yu
Summary: Differential hull clustering, i.e., the phenomenon that the differential probability of a cipher can exceed its best single trail by many orders of magnitude, has long been observed, but a structural explanation of where the clustering comes from has been missing. This paper gives such an explanation for four-bit nibble SPNs: the core-restricted clustering gap is governed by the recurrent cores of the round function, i.e. the irreducible recurrent components of the differential transition. For a core C with k active S-boxes and weighted adjacency matrix T_C of spectral radius ρ, the clustering gap obeys the asymptotic law gap_C(R) = R (µ(C) + log2 ρ) + O(1), where µ(C) is the minimum-mean-cycle weight. A central consequence is that the branch number, the standard diffusion metric, is not sufficient to bound clustering: it controls only the single-trail weight, not the trail multiplicity measured by ρ. We make the energy/entropy split rigorous through the variational principle, which identifies log2 ρ as an entropy term, and we show that for a periodic core the O(1) transient is the discrete Fourier transform of its cyclic classes; two branch-2 layers differ by 12.3 bits of gap while a branch-4 layer clusters less than both. We construct new differential distinguishers on CRAFT in the single-tweak model for 11 to 14 rounds; at each of these round counts, the probability of our distinguisher is, to our knowledge, the highest reported to date. The 11-round distinguisher reduces the data complexity from 2^49.79 to 2^49.559. We also report, to our knowledge, the first single-tweak differentials for 1 to 8 rounds. The theory is implemented in an open, C++-accelerated tool (coretool) that automates core search, spectral analysis and finite-round validation on CRAFT, GIFT-64, PRESENT-80, SKINNY-64 and controlled ablations, yielding actionable design guidelines for hull-resistant linear layers.

item.title: CycloSPDZ: Efficient MPC over 2-Power Cyclotomic Rings mod \(2^k\) for Dishonest Majority
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2972
Authors: Jianguo Xie, Yutao Sun, Jingqiang Lin, Nenghai Yu, Guozhen Shi
Summary: Most multi-party computation (MPC) protocols support arithmetic over finite fields or integer rings. Polynomial arithmetic in applications such as convolution evaluation and distributed key generation motivates extending these protocols to the 2-power cyclotomic rings $R_k=\mathbb{Z}_{2^k}[X]/(X^N+1)$, where $N$ is a power of two. However, no native protocol is known for actively secure computation over these rings with a dishonest majority.
In this work, we present an information-theoretic MAC that is homomorphic over $R_k$ and requires only a small increase in coefficient bit length. We apply this to construct CycloSPDZ, an actively secure MPC protocol for a dishonest majority in the preprocessing model that has efficiency comparable to the state-of-the-art field-based convolution protocols in Convolutions in Overdrive (PoPETs 2023). We also construct an efficient preprocessing protocol from authenticated integer-ring triples by adapting Toom–4 multiplication to power-of-two moduli via scaled interpolation and batched exact division, and combining it with Karatsuba multiplication in a hybrid scheme. As an application, we evaluate convolution workloads using polynomial encoding and blocking. We implement and benchmark the online phase of CycloSPDZ against our hybrid variant of SPD$\mathbb{Z}_{2^k}$ (CRYPTO 2018) and the function-dependent variant of the Matrix Rings (ASIACRYPT 2024), achieving speedups of up to $5\times$ and $48\times$, respectively.

item.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2971
Authors: David Tse, Nikhil Vanjani, Psi Vesely
Summary: Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation’s parameters.
Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{\lambda/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $\lambda$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.

item.title: Pretzel: Compact Lattice Signatures from Module-LWE and Module-SIS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2970
Authors: Alberto Centelles Hidalgo, Justin Thaler, Markos Georghiades
Summary: We present Pretzel, a lattice-based signature scheme in the style of ML-DSA. Across parameter sets targeting NIST security categories 2, 3, and 5, its signatures are 52-59% smaller than ML-DSA's, it signs and verifies faster in all three categories, and its quantum security proof needs fewer assumptions. Across all three parameter sets, Pretzel produces smaller signatures than SHUTTLE (Ming et al., ASIACRYPT 2026), the recent state of the art for iterative rejection sampling from Module-LWE. At category 3, for example, Pretzel's 1361-byte signatures are 14% smaller than SHUTTLE's 1589 bytes. Unlike the quantum analyses of ML-DSA and SHUTTLE, Pretzel's security proof in the quantum random oracle model needs no self-target assumption: it relies only on Module-LWE and Module-SIS. Like SHUTTLE, Pretzel builds on Gartner's iterative rejection sampling (CRYPTO 2025). Its sampler keeps the response exactly on its target distribution after every update, which allows a substantially narrower mask than SHUTTLE's. Its verifier also enforces an additional bound on the response coefficients. This bound lets the security proof adapt Poremba's LWE-phase technique (ITCS 2023) to Module-LWE and rely on Module-LWE and Module-SIS alone.

item.title: TreeOnion: Efficient Private Retrieval of Tree Paths
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2969
Authors: Pranav Shriram Arunachalaramanan, Chenyang Zhang, Yue Chen, Ling Ren
Summary: Private information retrieval (PIR) lets clients retrieve entries from a public database hosted on a server without revealing which entries are retrieved. Traditionally, the database is assumed to be an array or a key-value store, and the client has the index or keyword of the entry it wishes to retrieve. However, in practice, the database can have a more complex structure. An important example is when the database is organized as a tree, and the client wants to retrieve all nodes along a root-to-leaf path. Notably, retrieving a Merkle proof is a natural instance of this problem, as is done in applications such as certificate transparency and blockchain systems.
We present TreeOnion, a single-server scheme that allows clients to privately retrieve a path of nodes from a public database organized as a tree. For small node sizes, the communication and computation costs of TreeOnion are comparable to the costs of privately retrieving a single node from the same database.
